body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: The Lyceum goes on extremely well, except when the Manager of the English Opera produces a piece of his own, and then it undergoes a regular fit of dullness, as in the medley which appeared last Wednesday, and which is understood to be another of Mr. Arnold's annual contributions. This "new" piece, made after the good old Lagoda patent, is called, by way of attraction, the Devil’s Bridge; and is described by the author as an Operatic Romance, that is to say, a miscellany of speaking and pantomime, landscapes and dungeons, soldiers, lovers, fine clothes, songs, horrors, and merry andrews, virtue in distress, and wicked, inordinate barons in whiskers and half-boots. All these are to be found in the Devil's Bridge; and the reader will easily understand all that is to be found in it besides, when he obtains a hint of the story. There is a family of peasants then, who assist injured travellers,—a persecuted and peripatetic lady with her little boy—a lover in disguise, who turns out to be the husband of the lady just returned from the coast of Barbary,—a bravo, who deals in assassinations at the shortest notice,—and a baron seeking unlawfully to marry the said lady, while at the very same time (only think of the original scoundrel!) he has a wife of his own, all in a dungeon. The dialogue belonging to this venerable history, is of course in the possession of any reader who has frequented the theatre for the last ten or a dozen years, and so are the songs, with the exception perhaps of a little additional sprinkling of ahs! and ohs! with which Mr. Arnold seems to have been inspired in consequence of his late theatrical acquaintance with Mr. Moore, and which, he flatters himself no doubt, have given him all the graces of that gentleman's style. The only incident, with a shadow of novelty, is one in which Count Belino, the lover, disguised as a wandering artist, explains to the guilty Baron, his enemy, a drawing of his which had fallen into the latter's hands, and which to his great terror and rage, and to the ultimate detection of the Count, describes a main part of his iniquities. This is done by a song, which is composed by Mr. Braham in a style of great expressiveness and insinuation, and sung by him in a manner quite worthy the composition. The rest of the music by that Gentleman and Mr. Horn has little pretension to novelty or science. Two songs of the latter, in particular, which are sung with great spirit by Mrs. Dickons, are singularly deficient in expression, more than half of the music in both instances being directly contrary to the cast of the words,—playful when it should be in repose, and absolutely sprightly when it should be sad.

The principal novelty of the piece altogether is the appearance of a young Gentleman, who, according to a long puff for Mr. Arnold, in the Morning Chronicle, is the son of Signor Rovedino, and a pupil of Mr. Braham. His aspect is not prepossessing, nor his personal bearing indicative of a talent for acting; but his voice is melodious, firm, and of good compass; and he promises to do credit to his master,—singular credit indeed, if he remains, as at present, unspoiled by the vicious ornament of the latter, whose "purity of style" is certainly to be found nowhere but in the puff above-mentioned, whatever may be the case with respect to his "clearness of articulation."
